newsitem.title: FRANCE: France still tips in favour of EMU.
newsitem.headline: France still tips in favour of EMU.

text.p: France voted by a whisker in favour of European monetary union in a referendum four years ago, and if asked again, the result would probably not be much different.
The country is still divided on the merits of launching a single currency, but, like the narrow 51.05 percent majority backing it in 1992, polls show the balance still tips in favour.
Officially, France is committed to launching the single currency on time in 1999, but there is a sizeable minority of doubters which goes across political party lines.
The referendum, as former European Commission President Jacques Delors said at the time, "revealed a France with many faces, a France divided by multiple fault lines".
Those fault lines became glaringly obvious again this autumn in a renewed debate in France on the merits of monetary union.
It took just a few comments by an ex-president with little residual political clout to highlight France's schizophrenic approach to its forthcoming monetary marriage with Germany.
Ironically, they came from one of the founding fathers of the European Monetary System, Valery Giscard d'Estaing.
His call for a fall in the franc to boost growth inspired a revolt against a decade-old link to the mark and was echoed even inside the Bank of France, bastion of monetary orthodoxy.

Two members of the central bank's nine-member monetary policy council questioned the franc-mark link, long seen as the linchpin of the single currency project, prompting governor Jean-Claude Trichet to stress that he alone spoke for the bank.

While Giscard d'Estaing whipped up misgivings in the ruling centre-right coalition, a truck drivers' strike, partly caused by the effects of European competition, was paralysing roads and choking the economy.

That strike, ended by a government climbdown, followed a crippling public sector strike last December against government austerity policies meant to ensure France qualifies for monetary union at its launch in 1999.
Doubts about monetary union appear to have receded somewhat -- at least for now.
Officials have warned that there can be no going back.

"Given where we are now, in December 1996, and given what has been said and done already I don't believe, the single currency will not be launched," French Treasury director Jean Lemierre said last week. "It seems unimaginable to me."

"I think the 1999 date is inevitable. Failure to respect it would lead to such a crisis for our country and our economy that I cannot imagine this catastrophic scenario," European Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said last month.
But with unemployment at a record 12.6 percent, and economic growth sluggish, there is plenty of room for controversy to burst to the surface again.

President Jacques Chirac, who in his 1995 election campaign flirted with the idea of a new referendum on Europe, has worked hard since then to dispel doubts about the depth of his commitment to the euro.

Though few believe Chirac would want to go down in history as the president who derailed monetary union, he has not yet gained the stature of former president Francois Mitterrand who provided the political vision behind the single currency plan.
And he does not have as close a rapport with Kohl, which enabled Mitterrand to ensure the drive to European monetary union was based on a balanced Franco-German partnership.
That alliance is showing signs of strain at the moment.

At issue are different views on how to run the single currency -- with France insisting on political counterweight to the future European Central Bank and Germany, haunted by memories of hyper-inflation in the 1920s, looking for watertight guarantees on the stability of the euro.

Analysts say much hinges on whether France and Germany can find a balanced solution to a dispute over a budget discipline pact to ensure future monetary union members stick to fiscal rigour after 1999.
EU leaders are to discuss the so-called stability pact at a summit in Dublin this weekend.
"French people are paying a lot of attention at the moment to what will happen in Dublin," Bank of France monetary policy council member Paul Marchelli told Reuters this week.

For Eurosceptics, any Franco-German tension makes it easy to exploit lingering suspicion and fear of Germany in some quarters after several bitter wars. The Socialist opposition this week accused Chirac of capitulating to Kohl on the stability pact.

Philippe Seguin, who campaigned against the Maastricht treaty in the 1992 referendum, struck the same chord in 1993 when he compared government austerity policies and neglect of unemployment to a "social Munich" -- a reference to the pre-World War Two appeasement of Hitler.
Even for supporters of EMU, Germany's insistence on getting its own way on the stability pact undermines some of the reasons for backing the single currency in the first place.
France's prime motive in pushing for the single currency was a determination to regain a share of monetary sovereignty.
Without monetary union, it feared, Europe would be increasingly run by Germany, Europe's biggest economy, with the Bundesbank setting Europe-wide monetary policy.
So if it could not stand up to the Bundesbank, it could at least win a seat on the board by persuading Bonn and its other EU partners to set up a European Central Bank.

More recently officials have added a new concept to justify the single currency -- "globalisation", a fashionable buzzword used to sum up the idea that France can no longer compete alone in an increasingly interlinked world economy.
Euro-enthusiasts believe the euro will usher in currency stability, lower interest rates and create a trading zone the size of the United States, boosting jobs and growth.
Ironically, the latest debate on the merits of monetary union erupted just as the pressure of financial market scepticism about France's chances of qualifying for the single currency lifted.
It fulfils the Maastricht treaty criteria on debt, inflation, long-term interest rates and currency stability.
And it recently said it planned to use a transfer of pension fund money from state-owned France Telecom in 1997 to cut its budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product.
